title: A Student's Typical Week
paragraphs: Amir Bekzhanov is a second-year Computer Science student at WKU. His weekly routine is busy but well-organised. Every morning, he wakes up at 6:30 — not because he wants to, but because his first lecture starts at 8:00. He quickly showers, eats a light breakfast (usually toast and tea), and walks to the main building. The walk takes about twelve minutes, which he uses to listen to an English podcast. "I always listen to something in English," he says. "It helps me think in the language." By the time he arrives at the lecture hall, he already feels mentally active and ready to focus.

Amir's schedule varies from day to day, but certain habits stay the same. He always attends all his lectures — he never misses a class unless he is seriously ill. After each lecture, he spends fifteen minutes reviewing his notes while the information is still fresh. He does this without fail, even when he is tired. "If you review your notes immediately, you remember twice as much," he explains. "I learned that from a study skills course in my first year." He also keeps a small notebook where he writes down any word or phrase he doesn't understand — in any subject, not just English.

Three evenings a week, Amir studies in the WKU library from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. He sits at the same desk near the window, away from the noisy areas. He sometimes works on programming assignments, sometimes reads textbooks, and occasionally helps classmates who are struggling with code. He rarely uses his phone during library sessions — he puts it on silent and turns it face down. "Three hours of focused work is worth more than six hours of distracted work," he says. His classmates have noticed that he is one of the most productive students in the group, even though he doesn't appear to rush or panic.

Amir is also a member of the WKU Robotics Club, which meets every Wednesday at 5 p.m. for two hours. He finds this the most exciting part of his week. "In class, we learn the theory," he says. "In the club, we build things. It makes the theory real." The club is currently working on an autonomous navigation system for a small robot — Amir leads the software team. He believes that practical projects build skills that lectures alone cannot teach.

Nutrition and physical health are also part of Amir's system. He tries to eat a balanced diet during the week — the WKU canteen offers affordable meals, and he usually has soup and a main course for lunch. He occasionally cooks for himself on evenings when the canteen is closed, but he admits his cooking skills are basic. Exercise happens three times a week: he does a twenty-minute workout in his room on Monday and Thursday mornings, and plays football on Saturday afternoons. "I don't need a gym membership," he says. "Consistency matters more than equipment."

On weekends, Amir is more relaxed. He sleeps until 8:30, cooks a proper breakfast, and calls his parents in Aktobe. Saturday afternoons are for sport — he usually plays football with friends from his dormitory. Sunday is reserved for reading and planning. He reads both fiction and technical books: at the moment, he is working through a novel by Chinghiz Aitmatov in Russian and a book on machine learning in English. Sunday evening is planning time — he writes next week's tasks in his notebook and estimates how long each will take.

Amir's relationship with technology is intentional. He uses his phone as a tool, not as entertainment. Notifications are turned off for all social media apps during study hours. He checks messages twice a day — once at lunchtime and once in the evening. "Most messages are not urgent," he says. "And if something is truly urgent, people call." This approach is unusual among his peers, but Amir believes it saves him at least two hours every day.

Despite his busy schedule, Amir never feels overwhelmed. "The key is not to do everything at once," he says. "You plan the week on Sunday evening, you follow the plan, and you rest properly. Rest is not wasted time — it is part of the system." Many of his classmates wonder how he manages to do so much and still stay calm. His answer is always the same: "Consistency. Small habits, every single day. You don't need to be the most talented person in the room — you just need to show up, every single day, and do the work."

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Amir, how do you stay so organised? You always seem to have everything under control.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Honestly? I plan everything on Sunday. I write the week in my notebook — every task, every deadline.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: But don't you ever feel like you're missing out? Like, you never just relax spontaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I do relax — I just schedule it. Saturday football, Sunday reading. It's on the plan.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: That's so different from me. I always start things at the last minute.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: I used to do that too in school. But at university, it stopped working. There's just too much.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: What's the one thing you'd recommend to a first-year student?

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Review your notes on the same day. Fifteen minutes. Every single day. It changes everything.
